# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: Rise, Fall, and Re-emergence

## Introduction and rationale

Drug-eluting stents (DES) transformed percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) by reducing restenosis, yet a residual ongoing risk of stent-related adverse events persists. Despite improvements in restenosis with the evolution from balloon angioplasty to bare-metal stents and then DES, there remains a 2% to 3% per year incidence of stent-related events beyond 1 year, related in part to the permanent metallic frame, which distorts the vessel, limits vasomotion and adaptive remodelling, and serves as a nidus for chronic inflammation, neoatherosclerosis, thrombosis, and strut fracture [1]. Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were conceived to provide transient mechanical support and drug delivery, then disappear, restoring vascular structure and function [1,2].

## Early clinical experience

The first-in-human ABSORB study evaluated a fully bioabsorbable everolimus-eluting device. A fully bioabsorbable drug-eluting coronary stent that scaffolds the vessel wall when needed and then disappears has theoretical advantages; the device tested had a backbone of poly-L-lactic acid providing support and a coating of poly-D,L-lactic acid controlling release of everolimus [3]. Two-year imaging follow-up of this cohort further characterised resorption and vascular behaviour [4]. These encouraging early signals propelled the device into a large randomised programme.

## Pivotal randomised trials

The ABSORB II trial randomised patients 2:1 to the Absorb scaffold or Xience metallic stent. At 3 years the trial did not meet its co-primary endpoints of superior vasomotor reactivity and non-inferior late luminal loss; the metallic stent had significantly lower late luminal loss, and a higher rate of device-oriented composite endpoint due to target vessel myocardial infarction was observed in the Absorb group [5]. ABSORB Japan [6] and ABSORB China [7] confirmed short-term angiographic non-inferiority in regulatory cohorts.

The largest trial, ABSORB III, randomised 2,008 patients. The ABSORB III trial demonstrated noninferior rates of target lesion failure at 1 year in patients randomised to BVS versus cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents [8]. A patient-level pooled meta-analysis supported broadly comparable 1-year outcomes [9]. However, longer follow-up was less reassuring. In the ABSORB III trial, 3-year adverse event rates were higher with BVS than EES, particularly target vessel myocardial infarction and device thrombosis [10]. Critically, the temporal pattern mattered: cumulative 5-year adverse event rates were increased after BVS compared with everolimus-eluting stents, but the period of excess risk for BVS ended at 3 years, coincident with complete scaffold resorption [11].

The all-comers AIDA trial tested the scaffold in routine practice. There was no significant difference between groups in the primary outcome of target-vessel failure, but treatment with the bioresorbable scaffold was associated with a significantly higher incidence of overall and very late device thrombosis than the metallic stent through 2 years [12], a finding sustained at 5 years [13].

## Scaffold thrombosis: the central limitation

Multiple analyses converged on excess thrombotic risk. A two-year meta-analysis found that the excess risk of BVS relative to EES for stent thrombosis through 2 years was significant [14]. A meta-analysis of seven randomised trials with individual patient data reached similar conclusions on medium-term safety [15], as did weighted [16] and time-stratified analyses across all timepoints to 5 years [17]. A comprehensive network meta-analysis reinforced this: patients treated with the Absorb BVS had a significantly higher risk of definite or probable scaffold thrombosis compared with metallic DES, and the risk of very late scaffold thrombosis was highest with the Absorb BVS among comparators [18]. Mechanistic registries linked events to device factors and implantation technique [19], and procedural technique (predilatation, sizing, post-dilatation) emerged as a key modifiable determinant [20].

## Technique optimisation and ABSORB IV

Recognising that early trials enrolled small vessels and used suboptimal technique, ABSORB IV applied an improved implantation protocol in a blinded design. In earlier studies lesions smaller than intended were frequently enrolled, implantation technique was suboptimal, and patients with myocardial infarction were excluded [21]. With optimised technique, polymeric BVS implanted with optimised technique in an expanded patient population resulted in non-inferior 30-day and 1-year rates of target lesion failure and angina compared with metallic DES [22], with a low 1-year scaffold thrombosis rate [23]. Five-year ABSORB IV outcomes [24] and the final ABSORB programme report [25] provided long-term context.

## Commercial withdrawal

The accumulated safety signal had regulatory and commercial consequences. The 3-year outcome of ABSORB II, confirmed by meta-analyses, resulted in the end of Absorb BVS use in Europe and the United States, and in September 2017 Absorb BVS was withdrawn from the market [26]. Abbott halted sales of the Absorb scaffold as of September 14, 2017, attributing the decision to low commercial sales while pledging continued work on a next-generation device [27].

## Next-generation devices

Attention shifted to thinner-strut and metallic absorbable platforms. Higher scaffold thrombosis rates with first-generation scaffolds were likely due in part to insufficient radial strength necessitating larger strut profiles, so attention has focused on increasing tensile strength and reducing strut thickness [28]. The sirolimus-eluting magnesium scaffold (Magmaris) was evaluated in BIOSOLVE-II. BIOSOLVE-II evaluated Magmaris in 123 patients with de novo lesions, and at 6 months the in-segment late lumen loss was 0.27 ± 0.37 mm [29]. Lessons from earlier failures continue to inform iterative magnesium scaffold design [30].

## Conclusion

The BVS story is a cautionary tale of an elegant concept undermined by device-specific thrombotic risk. While first-generation polymeric scaffolds underperformed contemporary DES, the excess risk was confined to the period before resorption and was attenuated by patient selection and meticulous technique. Whether thinner-strut and absorbable-metal platforms can deliver the long-term promise of vascular restoration without compromising safety remains the central question for ongoing research.
